S67-F1-Q1.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
S67-F1-Q1.prompt:
Observational data show r = -0.6 between evening screen time and hours of sleep. To test cause, 50 volunteers were randomly assigned to no screens after 8 p.m. or to their usual habits. The no-screen group slept 0.5 hour more on average. In 1,000 random regroupings, a difference of at least 0.5 hour (no-screen minus usual) happened 2 times.
Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
S67-F1-Q1.correct_answer: Yes. 2 ÷ 1,000 = 0.2%, which is below 5%, so chance alone is very unlikely to explain it; cutting evening screens likely increased sleep for volunteers like these.
S67-F1-Q1.grading_note: Form required: the decision with the simulated proportion compared with 5%.

S67-F1-Q2.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
S67-F1-Q2.prompt: Why can this randomized experiment, but not the observational correlation alone, support the claim that evening screens reduce sleep?
S67-F1-Q2.correct_answer: Random assignment tends to balance other variables (such as stress or age) between the groups, so a significant difference can be credited to the treatment; in observational data a lurking variable could explain the correlation.
S67-F1-Q2.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that contrasts random assignment with possible lurking variables.

S67-F1-Q3.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
S67-F1-Q3.prompt:
In a randomization test, the observed difference was matched or exceeded in 350 of 1,000 regroupings.
Using a 5% threshold, what is the conclusion?
choices: The treatment definitely has no effect.
The difference is not significant; chance could easily explain it.
S67-F1-Q3.correct_answer: The difference is not significant; chance could easily explain it.
S67-F1-Q3.grading_note: 350 ÷ 1,000 = 35%, far above 5%. A non-significant result does not prove there is no effect.

S67-F1-Q4.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
S67-F1-Q4.prompt: In a randomization test, the regroupings show how large the difference between groups tends to be when the treatment has no effect.
S67-F1-Q4.grading_note: Regrouping the same results at random imitates assignment with no treatment effect.

S67-F1-Q5.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether an association is causal
S67-F1-Q5.prompt: If an experiment's difference is not significant, that proves the treatment has no effect.
S67-F1-Q5.grading_note: It means the data do not show an effect beyond chance; a small effect could still exist.

S67-F2-Q1.skill: Evaluate claims based on a correlation
S67-F2-Q1.prompt:

S67-F2-Q1.correct_answer: r is not a percent of change (r² ≈ 0.36 describes the share of variation explained), and correlation does not show causation.

S67-F2-Q2.skill: Evaluate claims based on a correlation
S67-F2-Q2.prompt:

Why should you be cautious?

S67-F2-Q3.skill: Evaluate claims based on a correlation
S67-F2-Q3.prompt: Which statement about r = -0.9 is correct?

The slope of the line is -0.9.
90% of the points are on the line.
An increase in x causes y to fall.
S67-F2-Q3.correct_answer: There is a strong negative linear association.
S67-F2-Q3.grading_note: r measures the direction and strength of a linear association only.

S67-F2-Q4.skill: Evaluate claims based on a correlation
S67-F2-Q4.prompt: A correlation can be strong even when the relationship is not causal.
S67-F2-Q4.grading_note: A lurking variable can create it.

S67-F2-Q5.skill: Evaluate claims based on a correlation
S67-F2-Q5.prompt: If r = 0.8, the slope of the least-squares line is 0.8.
S67-F2-Q5.grading_note: The slope depends on the units and spreads of x and y.

S68-B2-Q1.skill: Use random samples to make valid generalizations
S68-B2-Q1.prompt: Why is a random sample more likely to represent a population than a convenience sample?
S68-B2-Q1.correct_answer: Every member has the same chance of being chosen, so the method does not favor any group (no selection bias), although a random sample can still differ from the population by chance.

S68-B2-Q2.skill: Use random samples to make valid generalizations
S68-B2-Q2.prompt:
A survey at a gym asks about the exercise habits of all town residents.
What is the problem?
S68-B2-Q2.correct_answer: People at a gym probably exercise more than other residents, so the sample is biased.

S68-B2-Q3.skill: Use random samples to make valid generalizations
S68-B2-Q3.prompt: Which is a random sample of a school's students?
choices: Drawing 40 names from a list of all students
Asking the first 40 students in line
S68-B2-Q3.correct_answer: Drawing 40 names from a list of all students
S68-B2-Q3.grading_note: Only the drawing gives every student the same chance.

S68-B2-Q4.skill: Use random samples to make valid generalizations
S68-B2-Q4.prompt: Generalizations about a population are valid only if the sample represents the population.
S68-B2-Q4.grading_note: This is why random sampling matters.

S68-B2-Q5.skill: Use random samples to make valid generalizations
S68-B2-Q5.prompt: A sample of volunteers is a random sample.
